meta.title: Who really said "Out of suffering have emerged the strongest souls; the most massive characters are seared with scars"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Kahlil Gibran. The line is from preacher Edwin Hubbell Chapin’s 1853 Discourses on the Beatitudes, misattributed to Gibran only in the 20th century.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Out of suffering have emerged the strongest souls; the most massive characters are seared with scars'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Kahlil Gibran. The words are Edwin Hubbell Chapin’s, from his 1853 Discourses on the Beatitudes — a documented misattribution.

answer.label: Not Kahlil Gibran — actually Edwin Hubbell Chapin
answer.sourceLine: These words were written by the 19th-century American preacher Edwin Hubbell Chapin in his Discourses on the Beatitudes (1853), in the sermon “The Blessing of the Mourners.” They are documented to Chapin by the WIST quotation archive ↗ and only became attached to Kahlil Gibran much later, after being wrongly folded into a 20th-century Gibran anthology. There is no work of Gibran’s that contains this line.

source.heading: The real source
source.excerpt: Out of suffering have emerged the strongest souls; the most massive characters are seared with scars.
trail: The WIST quotation archive ↗ attributes the exact wording to Edwin Hubbell Chapin, Discourses on the Beatitudes, ch. 2 “The Blessing of the Mourners” (1853).
A researcher’s essay, “Kahlil Gibran and the Words He Never Said” ↗, traces how the line drifted from Chapin to Gibran and concludes Gibran “never said them.”
Chapin’s book survives in full as a scanned public-domain edition on HathiTrust ↗, confirming an 1850s first publication.
source.excerptNote: The line is drawn from a longer passage in Chapin’s sermon on Matthew 5:4; it is frequently quoted alone. The word in Chapin’s text is “seared” (some later reprints read “seamed”).

author.name: Edwin Hubbell Chapin
author.heading: About Edwin Hubbell Chapin
author.bio: Edwin Hubbell Chapin was a hugely popular American Universalist minister and orator, famed in mid-19th-century New York for the eloquence of his sermons and lectures. He published several volumes of discourses, including Discourses on the Beatitudes (1853), whose polished, aphoristic style is exactly what later made one of his sentences easy to mistake for the work of a lyric poet.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone says Gibran
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s most persistent Kahlil Gibran misquotes — feel-good, poetic, and pinned to a famous name. But it predates Gibran’s writing career and belongs to a 19th-century preacher.

items.why: Repeated across Goodreads ↗, BrainyQuote and countless social posts as Gibran’s, but it appears in none of his actual works. The misattribution ↗ spread after the line was folded into 20th-century Gibran compilations.

misattribution.truthLine: The author is Edwin Hubbell Chapin, who wrote the sentence in Discourses on the Beatitudes (1853), as documented by the WIST archive ↗ — decades before Gibran published anything.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The sentiment — that hardship forges the strongest character — reads perfectly in Gibran’s aphoristic voice, which is much of why the misattribution stuck. But Chapin was making a specifically consoling, pulpit point: preaching on “Blessed are they that mourn,” he cast suffering as the crucible of the greatest souls.

Stripped of its sermon context and re-badged with a poet’s name, the line lost its author but kept its comfort — a textbook example of how a striking sentence outlives the person who actually wrote it.
